title: AMF: N1N2MessageSubscribe response timeout may orphan stored subscriptions
body:
### Summary

When the AMF handles an N1N2MessageSubscribe, the HTTP thread hands the work to `TASK_AMF_APP` and blocks on a future for at most `KFutureStatusTimeoutMs` (1000 ms). If the APP task does not answer within that second, the HTTP thread returns an error to the client. But the APP task, when it does run, first stores the subscription in `n1n2_message_subscribe` and only then fills the promise. A subscription that misses the deadline is therefore kept by the AMF while the client is told the request failed.

The client never receives the subscription ID (the `Location` header), so it can never call `remove_n1n2_message_subscription()`, which is keyed by that ID. The subscription is unreachable and is freed only when the whole AMF exits. Unlike the AMF/SMF PDU-session leaks, nothing overwrites it — each missed request adds a new, permanently orphaned entry.

The PoC reproduces this on a live AMF: 120 subscribe requests issued while the APP task is stalled, 120 stored, 39 answered with `201`, and 81 orphaned.


### Details

Source analysis on `v2.2.1` (April 2026), AMF commit `513c0f2`.

**1. The HTTP thread waits one second, then gives up**

https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/513c0f2dc4175e7d8f099a41d4a797913d3cf40e/src/sbi/amf_http2_server.cpp#L1132-L1150

The handler creates a promise, sends `itti_sbi_n1n2_message_subscribe` to `TASK_AMF_APP`, and calls `wait_for_result(f, result_opt)`. That helper waits a single `KFutureStatusTimeoutMs` and returns `nullopt` on timeout (`oai-cn5g-common-src`, `utils/utils.hpp:18,32-46`). On `nullopt` the handler responds with an error and stops waiting.

**2. The APP task stores the subscription before it answers**

https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/513c0f2dc4175e7d8f099a41d4a797913d3cf40e/src/amf-app/amf_app.cpp#L862-L890

`add_n1n2_message_subscription()` (`:870`) inserts into the map first; `trigger_process_response()` (`:889`) fills the promise last. If the HTTP thread has already timed out, the insert has still happened and the promise-fill has no one listening.

https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/513c0f2dc4175e7d8f099a41d4a797913d3cf40e/src/amf-app/amf_app.cpp#L2119-L2127

**3. Cleanup needs the ID the client never got**

https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/513c0f2dc4175e7d8f099a41d4a797913d3cf40e/src/amf-app/amf_app.cpp#L2130-L2139

`remove_n1n2_message_subscription()` erases by `(ue_ctx_id, sub_id)`. The subscription ID is returned to the client only in the `201` `Location` header, which a timed-out request never sends. With no ID, the client cannot unsubscribe, and no other path removes the entry.

**What makes the APP task miss the deadline.** `TASK_AMF_APP` is single-threaded. Any handler that blocks it for ≥1 s pushes queued subscribe requests past their own timeout. One such path exists in-tree: `get_nrfs()` (`amf_app.cpp:2623`), reached from `update_amf_configuration` → `register_to_nrf()`, waits on an NSSF response per configured slice when `enable_nssf` is set. If the NSSF does not answer, each wait runs the full `KFutureStatusTimeoutMs`. Other operational causes — CPU-constrained node, scheduling pressure — produce the same effect without any specific code path.

### PoC

On `oai-amf:v2.2.1`, no source change.

**How the AMF is made to miss the deadline.** A subscribe only leaks if `TASK_AMF_APP` is busy when it arrives. `enable_nssf` is turned on and a fake `oai-nssf` is placed on the network that accepts TCP connections but never sends a reply. An AMF configuration `PUT` reaches `get_nrfs()`, which waits on that NSSF and runs the full 1000 ms timeout. Measured: the `PUT` returns `504` after `1.038 s`, and the AMF log shows the NSSF request at `02:38:20.061` with the next inbound request at `02:38:21.062` and nothing in between — the task really is stalled for that second.

**What is sent.** Three identical cycles. In each, the configuration `PUT` is looped to keep the task stalled, and 40 N1N2MessageSubscribe requests are sent at 0.1 s intervals for the same UE. Nothing is ever unsubscribed.

**What is counted.** On the client, the HTTP status of each of the 40 requests. On the AMF, the map size as (`Add an N1N2 Message Subscribe`) minus (`Remove an N1N2 Message Subscribe`) in the log. The two are counted separately so the AMF's view and the client's view can be compared.

```
                  map size | sent | 201 | 504 (timed out)
start                    0 |      |     |
after cycle 1           40 |   40 |  13 |  27
after cycle 2           80 |   40 |  13 |  27
after cycle 3          120 |   40 |  13 |  27
after 30 s idle        120 |      |     |

total: 120 sent, 39 x 201, 81 x 504, 0 removals logged
```

**The leak.** All 40 requests per cycle land in the map, but only 13 of them got a `201`. The other 27 got a `504`: the HTTP thread had already given up, so no `Location` header was sent and the client holds no subscription ID. The AMF kept them anyway — the insert happens before the promise is filled. Over three cycles that is 81 entries the AMF stores and the client cannot name. Since `remove_n1n2_message_subscription()` takes only that ID, nothing can ever delete them, which is why the removal count stays at 0.

**The accumulation.** The map rises by exactly 40 each cycle, never less. Subscription IDs are generated fresh per request, so a repeat subscribe for the same UE creates a new entry instead of replacing the old one — retrying does not clean up. And the count is unchanged 30 s later, so there is no expiry either. The only bound is the lifetime of the AMF process.

### Impact

The subscription stays in `n1n2_message_subscribe` for the life of the AMF process. The client believes the request failed and holds no ID, so `remove_n1n2_message_subscription()` can never target it; the AMF/SMF PDU-session leaks are at least overwritten on retry, but here each missed request adds a fresh, permanent entry.

Reaching the timeout needs the APP task blocked for a second. The clearest in-tree trigger is `get_nrfs()` waiting on an unresponsive NSSF, which requires `enable_nssf` and a reconfiguration; more generally, a CPU-constrained or overloaded AMF reaches the same window without any special path. Whenever that window overlaps NF subscribe traffic, orphaned subscriptions accumulate.

The growth is not bounded by an identity space the way the PDU-session maps are: subscription IDs are freshly generated per request, so the map grows with the number of timed-out subscribes over the AMF's lifetime.
